summary: This is a humorous RFC. It imagines an "Internet Protocol Police" charged with punishing willful violations of the "Collected Wisdom of the IETF community", and it sets out a schedule of punishments for such infractions. It is Informational and is not a real protocol specification.

plainLanguage.summary: It is a joke rulebook for pretend internet police, listing silly penalties for breaking the unwritten rules of the people who design the internet.

subtitle: A tongue-in-cheek schedule of penalties for breaking IETF community norms.

tldr.problem: The IETF community has informal norms and expectations for protocol design, but there has been no formal specification of how violations are handled.
tldr.mechanism: This April 1st humor document playfully establishes a schedule of punishments ranging from raised eyebrows for minor infractions like grammar mistakes to the legendary head-in-hand gesture for the most severe protocol design sins.
tldr.outcome: The joke illustrates that IETF review is subjective and peer pressure is real, while poking fun at reviewers who apply vague feedback like 'this needs elaboration' to steer protocol authors toward better designs.

facts.label: Punishments defined
facts.value: 5 (Raised Eyebrow, Frown, Shaking of the Head, Finger Wag, Head-in-Hand Gesture)

today: This is an April Fools' joke document published on April 1, 2026, and should not be deployed. It offers a humorous view of informal IETF review practices.

sections.title: The Internet Protocol Police
sections.content: This April 1st document imagines an Internet Protocol Police (IPP) whose job is to punish violations of the Collected Wisdom of the IETF community. The RFC is deliberately humorous and not a real protocol specification. The document publishes a formal schedule of punishments, which the community has applied informally for years.
sections.plainLanguage: The document jokes about a pretend police force that hands out punishments when people break the unwritten rules of protocol design.

sections.title: The Schedule of Punishments
sections.content: The IPP's punishment system ranges from mild to severe. The Raised Eyebrow is for minor infractions like bad grammar or inconsistent terminology. The Frown applies to serious mistakes such as using unregistered IANA codepoints or writing ABNF that cannot be parsed with 1993-era technology. The Shaking of the Head addresses hidden complexity, like case-folding without Unicode considerations. The rarest and most feared is The Head-in-Hand Gesture, rumored to have been invoked only once by an early greybeard who fully grasped the implications of HTML and HTTP.
sections.plainLanguage: The joke has five punishments. The smallest is just a disapproving look. The bigger ones are for when someone makes a really bad design choice. The scariest one is so rare that nobody has actually seen it happen.

sections.title: Percussive Persuasion During Development
sections.content: While protocols are being developed, experienced reviewers offer percussive persuasion through verbal utterances, not actual punishments. Phrases like 'This part needs elaboration' signal a missing explanation. 'You may have failed to consider...' means the reviewer sees a security attack the author did not defend against. 'The threat model seems underdeveloped' implies the author does not understand their own design. 'This may work in the lab, but...' flags missing operational considerations. The harshest is 'You have not thought this through', which is code for 'start over'. Despite rumors, wet noodles have never been part of the official process.
sections.plainLanguage: While someone is still writing the protocol, senior people give hints using special phrases. These are not official punishments, but they are serious warnings that something is wrong.
